gates.name: Porta Mugonia (Mucionis)

phases.t: Temple of Jupiter Stator vowed at the gate (Livy 10.36.11).

gates.note: Old gate of the Palatine at the summa Sacra Via by the temple of Jupiter Stator, where the Clivus Palatinus later climbed (Varro LL 5.164; Livy 1.12.3, Dionysius 2.50.3). Placed just SW of the Arch of Titus. End date arbitrary: the site was rebuilt after the fire of 64.

gates.name: Porta Romanula
gates.note: Palatine gate on the Velabrum side with steps down to the Nova Via by the sacellum of Volupia (Varro LL 5.164; 6.24); Platner places it a little south of S. Teodoro, at the foot of the Clivus Victoriae.

gates.name: Scalae Caci (Palatine stair-gate)
gates.note: The stair from the Forum Boarium up to the Germalus by the hut of Romulus; treated by Carandini as the third entrance of the archaic circuit. Stair remains near the Casa Romuli.

gates.name: Porta Pandana (Saturnia)
gates.note: Gate of the old Capitoline fortress, 'always open' (Festus; Varro LL 5.42 calls it Saturnia, from the old name of the hill); placed where the Clivus Capitolinus reached the hilltop. End date arbitrary.

gates.name: Porta Carmentalis

phases.t: The 306 Fabii leave by the right-hand arch (Livy 2.49.8; Ovid Fasti 2.201-204).
Rebuilt with the Grotta Oscura circuit.

gates.note: At the SW foot of the Capitol by the shrine of Carmenta, at the west end of the Vicus Iugarius (near the modern Anagrafe, Via Petroselli). Two passages; the right-hand one (Porta Scelerata) shunned after the Fabii marched out to the Cremera in 477 BC. Probably the gate passed by triumphs if it is not identical with the Porta Triumphalis. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

gates.name: Porta Triumphalis (location debated)
gates.note: Triumphal processions entered the city by the Porta Triumphalis (Cicero, In Pisonem 55; Suetonius, Aug. 100; Tacitus, Ann. 1.8). Theories: (1) a gate of the Servian Wall between the Carmentalis and the river near Sant'Omobono, used only for triumphs (placed here; the Italian Wikipedia list follows this); (2) one arch of the double Porta Carmentalis (Coarelli); (3) a free-standing ceremonial arch in the Campus Martius by the Circus Flaminius and Villa Publica (Haselberger; Richardson); (4) not a fixed structure at all. Point is illustrative only.

gates.name: Porta Flumentana

phases.t: Flood reaches the gate (Livy 35.9.3; 35.21.5).

gates.note: Gate toward the river between the temple of Portunus and the Tiber, where the road from the Pons Aemilius (Via Aurelia) entered; sometimes flooded (Livy 35.9.3). Whether it stood in a continuous wall is unknown.

gates.name: Porta Trigemina

phases.t: Porticus built from the gate to the Tiber (Livy 35.10.12).
Arch restored by the consuls (CIL VI 1385).

gates.note: Triple gate at the NW foot of the Aventine between the Forum Boarium and the river, by the Salinae; start of the Via Ostiensis and the Clivus Publicius. The 3.30 m arch found in 1885 near S. Maria in Cosmedin was proposed for it but is rejected by Platner. Inside the city by Augustus; arch restored by Lentulus and Crispinus (AD 2).

gates.name: Porta Lavernalis
gates.note: Aventine gate named from the altar of Laverna, perhaps beneath Sant'Anselmo, leading to the Via Ostiensis (Varro LL 5.163).

gates.name: Porta Raudusculana
gates.note: Gate in the saddle between the two Aventine summits at Piazza Albania, said to have been bronze-clad (raudus); a road (Vicus Portae Raudusculanae) led from it to the Ostiensis. The Viale Aventino stretch with the 87 BC catapult arch is just east.

gates.name: Porta Naevia
gates.note: Gate between S. Saba and S. Balbina at the southern corner of the Lesser Aventine, leading to the Via Ardeatina (Varro LL 5.163).

gates.name: Porta Capena

phases.t: Via Appia begun from the gate.
Footway paved from the gate to the temple of Mars (Livy 10.23.12).
Aqua Marcia carried over the gate.
Antoniniana branch to the Baths of Caracalla.

gates.note: Gate between the Caelian and the Aventine at the head of the Via Appia and Via Latina, between the Circus Maximus valley and Via delle Terme di Caracalla. The arcade of the Aqua Marcia (and later the Antonine branch) passed over it, so that it dripped ('madida Capena', Juvenal 3.11; Martial 3.47.1).

gates.name: Porta Caelimontana

phases.t: Rebuilt as the Arch of Dolabella and Silanus (consuls of AD 10).
Arcus Neroniani built over it.

gates.note: On the Caelian near S. Maria in Domnica; replaced in AD 10 by the travertine Arch of Dolabella and Silanus (CIL VI 1384), later used by Nero's branch of the Aqua Claudia (Arcus Neroniani). Faces roughly SE.

gates.name: Porta Querquetulana
gates.note: Gate named from an oak grove, probably near S. Clemente between the Caelian and Oppius, at the head of the road that became the Via Tusculana / Asinaria (Pliny NH 16.37).

gates.name: Porta Esquilina

phases.t: Sulla forces his way into the city here (Appian BC 1.58).
Rebuilt as the Arch of Gallienus and Salonina.

gates.note: At the top of the Clivus Suburanus on Via di S. Vito, start of the Via Labicana, Praenestina and Tiburtina; outside lay the Esquiline necropolis and puticuli. In 262 the gate was rebuilt as the travertine Arch of Gallienus (single surviving bay of an original three; about 8.8 m high) dedicated by M. Aurelius Victor (CIL VI 1106).

gates.name: Porta Viminalis
gates.note: The only gate through the agger, in Piazza dei Cinquecento just north of the surviving stretch; reached by the Vicus Patricius and Vicus Collis Viminalis.

gates.name: Porta Collina

phases.t: Gauls defeated before the gate (Livy 7.11).
Hannibal rides up to the gate (Livy 26.10.3).
Battle of the Colline Gate: Sulla defeats the Samnites and Marians (1 November 82 BC).

gates.note: North-east corner of the circuit at the corner of Via XX Settembre and Via Goito (site of the Ministry of Finance), where the Alta Semita and Vicus Longus met; start of the Via Salaria and Via Nomentana. Vestals convicted of unchastity were buried alive just inside at the Campus Sceleratus. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

gates.name: Porta Quirinalis
gates.note: Gate near the temple of Quirinus on the north edge of the Quirinal, near Via delle Quattro Fontane (Festus 303 L).

gates.name: Porta Salutaris
gates.note: Gate named from the temple of Salus, at the head of Via della Dataria (the Clivus Salutis).

gates.name: Porta Sanqualis
gates.note: Gate named from the shrine of Semo Sancus, at Largo Magnanapoli (wall remains in the central bed). Lost in the Trajanic works on the Quirinal slope (end date assumed). Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

gates.name: Porta Fontinalis

phases.t: Porticus from the gate to the Ara Martis in the Campus (Livy 35.10.12).

gates.note: On the saddle between the Arx and the Quirinal, in front of the Museo del Risorgimento: the Clivus Argentarius led up to it and the Via Lata / Flaminia began outside, past the tomb of Bibulus. In 193 BC a porticus was built from the gate to the altar of Mars (Livy 35.10.12). Destroyed with the saddle for Trajan's Forum (end date assumed). Perhaps the Porta Ratumena of the earlier wall. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

gates.name: Porta Ratumena
gates.note: Gate of the Arx toward the Campus Martius, named from the Veientine charioteer Ratumenna (Plutarch, Poplicola 13; Pliny NH 8.161). Possibly the predecessor of the Porta Fontinalis. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

gates.name: Porta Catularia
gates.note: Known from Festus (39 L) as a gate near the Capitol where red dogs were sacrificed; placed at the foot of the Capitol near the Carmentalis. Site wholly uncertain.

gates.name: Porta Flaminia

phases.t: Built with the wall: single arch between two towers.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): travertine facing and raised towers.
Witiges tries the gate; Belisarius holds it (Procopius 5.23.3).

gates.note: Northern gate on the Via Flaminia at the foot of the Pincian, beside the river wall. Honorian gate with a single travertine arch between two semicircular towers; the present Porta del Popolo facade is of 1562-65 and its towers of Sixtus IV (1475). Faces north.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Pinciana

phases.t: Postern.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): upgraded to a gate with two semicircular towers.
Belisarius holds the Pinciana and Salaria sector.

gates.note: Gate on the Via Salaria Vetus (Via Pinciana), originally a postern; given travertine facing and two semicircular towers by Honorius. Belisarius' command post during the siege (Procopius 5.19.14); the medieval legend of Belisarius begging here.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Salaria

phases.t: Built over tombs of the Via Salaria.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): raised, travertine facing.
24 August 410: Alaric enters here.
Main Gothic assault on the north side (Procopius 5.22.1).

gates.note: Gate of the Via Salaria Nova, demolished in 1871 after damage in the 1870 assault and rebuilt by Vespignani (removed 1921). Single arch between semicircular towers; tombs (Q. Sulpicius Maximus) found in the towers.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Nomentana

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): travertine facing and semicircular towers.

gates.note: Gate of the Via Nomentana, 75 m east of Michelangelo's Porta Pia (1561-65), which replaced it; walled up by Pius IV in 1564. The right tower survives; the left was demolished in 1827. Single arch between semicircular towers (Honorian travertine).
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Postern west of the Castra Praetoria (Via Montebello)
gates.note: One of the posterns near the Porta Nomentana and the camp's NW corner closed under Honorius (it.wikipedia, Mura aureliane). Position approximate.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: North gate of the Castra Praetoria (walled)

phases.t: Camp gate.
Blocked, open no longer.

gates.note: Gate of the praetorian camp in the north side, walled up when Aurelian absorbed the camp; the blocked arch is still visible. OSM labels it Porta Praetoriana.

gates.name: East gate of the Castra Praetoria (walled)

phases.t: Camp gate.
Blocked.

gates.note: East gate of the camp (Porta Principalis Dextera in OSM), blocked when the camp entered the Aurelian circuit.

gates.name: Porta Chiusa (Porta Clausa)

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Possibly closed in the Honorian works.

gates.note: Gate on Viale Pretoriano south of the camp, closed already in antiquity (name medieval); single arch flanked by a square tower. Probably the end of the Vicus Collis Viminalis road.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Tiburtina

phases.t: Augustan aqueduct arch over the road.
Aqueduct arch becomes the gate.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): outer gate court and facade, inscription naming Arcadius and Honorius, at the suggestion of Stilicho.

gates.note: Gate of the Via Tiburtina built against the travertine arch that carried the Aquae Marcia, Tepula and Julia over the road (Augustus, 5 BC; restored by Titus and Caracalla). Honorius added an outer travertine gatehouse with a single arch and square towers and the dedication of 401-402 (CIL VI 1189). Porta S. Lorenzo in the Middle Ages.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Praenestina-Labicana (Porta Maggiore)

phases.t: Claudian aqueduct crossing built.
Becomes a gate of the wall.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): outer gate with towers over the Eurysaces tomb; inscription CIL VI 1188.
Witiges' main camp opposite; Gothic assault at the Vivarium just south (Procopius 5.22-23).

gates.note: Double arch of the Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus over the forking Via Praenestina and Via Labicana (AD 52, travertine, rusticated, attic with the inscriptions of Claudius, Vespasian 71 and Titus 81), turned into a two-bay gate in 271. Honorius built an outer gatehouse with towers over the tomb of Eurysaces (demolished 1838). One of the two gates (with the Portuensis) to keep two bays. Height to the top of the attic about 24 m.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Asinaria

phases.t: Postern-type gate.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): semicircular towers added.
Belisarius enters Rome (9-10 December).
Betrayed to Totila (Procopius 7.20.14-19).

gates.note: Gate on the Via Asinaria next to the later Porta S. Giovanni (1574). Originally a postern with a single travertine arch; Honorius added two semicircular towers and a gatehouse. Through it Belisarius entered in 536 and Totila's Goths were let in by Isaurian guards on 17 December 546.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Metrovia (Metronia)
gates.note: Postern at the bend of the wall below the Caelian where the Marrana stream passed under the wall; mentioned by Gregory the Great (Epist. 9.69 'porta Metrovia'). Single small arch beside a square tower.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Latina

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): travertine arch, towers raised.
Walled up during the siege? (uncertain).

gates.note: Gate of the Via Latina with a single travertine arch (keystone with chi-rho on the outer face, Honorian or later) flanked by semicircular towers; the inner face is brick. Close to the church of S. Giovanni a Porta Latina.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Appia (Porta San Sebastiano)

phases.t: Double-arched gate, semicircular towers.
Honorian rebuild: single arch, attic, square tower bases.
Greek inscription to SS Conon and George (6th-7th century).

gates.note: The grandest gate, on the Via Appia. Aurelian's gate had two arches and two semicircular towers with a travertine facade; Honorius (401-402) reduced it to one arch, added a high attic with two rows of six windows and an open crenellated walkway, set the towers on square marble-faced bases, and joined them to the 'Arch of Drusus' (the arch of the Aqua Antoniniana) behind by two walls forming a courtyard. A storey was added later. Towers here estimated at about 26 m.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Ardeatina
gates.note: Minor gate on the Via Ardeatina, between the Appia and the Ostiensis; obliterated by Antonio da Sangallo's bastion (1537-42). Simple arch without towers. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Ostiensis (Porta San Paolo)

phases.t: Double outer arch.
Single outer arch, towers raised, inner double-arched court.
Opened to Totila by the Isaurians (Procopius 7.36.7).

gates.note: Gate of the Via Ostiensis beside the Pyramid of Cestius. Aurelian's outer facade had two arches between semicircular towers; Honorius reduced the outer face to one arch, raised the towers and added an inner court whose city face keeps two arches. Totila took Rome when Isaurian guards opened it (549/550).
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Museo della Via Ostiense (Porta S. Paolo)

gates.name: Postern west of the Pyramid of Cestius
gates.note: Postern in the stretch between the Pyramid and the Tiber, closed by Maxentius and demolished in 1888 (it.wikipedia, Mura aureliane). Position approximate. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Portuensis

phases.t: Two-arched gate.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): two arches retained, gate and towers raised.

gates.note: Southern gate of the Trastevere salient at the start of the Via Portuensis and Via Campana, at the junction of Via Portuense and Via E. Bezzi, about 450 m south of Porta Portese (1644) which replaced it when Urban VIII demolished the Janiculum walls. Honorius kept two arches, raised gate and towers and set up an inscription like those of the Tiburtina and Praenestina (CIL VI 1190). Tower form assumed.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Aurelia (Porta San Pancrazio)

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Held by Paulus during the siege (Procopius 5.18.35, 5.23.12).

gates.note: Gate on the Janiculum summit where the Via Aurelia Vetus left Trastevere, called Porta S. Pancratii from the 6th century (Procopius 5.18.35). Destroyed in the 1849 siege and rebuilt by Vespignani (1854). Tower form unknown. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Septimiana
gates.note: Northern gate of the Trastevere salient at the start of Via della Lungara; the name may recall Septimius Severus (the Horti Getae nearby). Rebuilt in 1498 by Alexander VI with Ghibelline merlons.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: Porta Aurelia-Sancti Petri (Porta Cornelia)
gates.note: River-wall gate at the left-bank end of the Pons Aelius, through which the road to the Vatican and the Via Cornelia passed; Procopius' 'Aurelian gate, now named after Peter' (5.19.4). Covered after 403 by the fortified Mausoleum of Hadrian across the river. Form unknown.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: River postern at Tor di Nona
gates.note: One of the small landing-stage posterns of the Campus Martius river wall; the medieval Torre dell'Annona (Tor di Nona) stood on the wall here. Some identify a 'Porta Domitia' near it.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)

gates.name: River postern near the Mausoleum of Augustus
gates.note: Posterula in the river wall opposite the Mausoleum of Augustus, where river traffic landed (later Porto di Ripetta). Illustrative position.
